conditions: Every engine runs in Docker under an identical cpuset and memory cap, one job at a time, on the same host.

Peak memory is the largest amount an engine held in its own address space, added over every container a run used, and it leaves out the file cache the kernel keeps on the engine's behalf. That is the right number for engines that manage their own memory, and an undercount for engines that lean on the kernel instead, so compare it down one engine's rows rather than across engines that work differently.
Each printed cell is the median of 5 repetitions, with min and max carried alongside; nothing here is a single sample.
Defaults first. Where a default would make the comparison meaningless, it is equalized and the override is disclosed rather than hidden.
Comparators are pinned by sha256 image digest, not by a floating tag.
provenance_note: Some benchmarks record which machine they ran on and some record only the container, so that column is filled in where it was measured and left alone where it was not. Everything on this page ran on the same machine; this note reports what each result can actually show rather than what we know to be true of all of them.

tables.title: Graph OLTP
conditions: Disk is what the workload left on disk, in GiB: the engine's writable layer plus its volumes after the cell, minus the same engine's empty footprint.
There is no cold column on this table, and the reason is recorded on the rows themselves: no cold/warm split: each operation runs against an already-built, already-warm database by construction

Durability is matched at the relaxed end: on every engine that has the setting, a commit returns without waiting for the disk and the log is flushed by the engine's own background policy, which is ArcadeDB's engine default and a documented production mode for each of the others. Every engine's setting was read out of the engine rather than assumed, and each row records what it ran as `durability`. The exception on this table is DuckPGQ, LadybugDB, and Neo4j, which have no setting to relax and wait for the disk at every commit; their write and transaction cells are paying for that. SurrealDB (server) exposes no durability setting at all and what it does at commit could not be established, so it is in neither class and its row says so rather than claiming one.
Every engine traverses the same persons-and-KNOWS projection, with edges stored in both directions.

ArcadeDB (embedded), ArcadeDB (server), and Neo4j run on a JVM, and for them this column is close to the heap they were given rather than the memory the work needed: Neo4j's 4.74 GiB here is about 119 per cent of its 4g heap, and across every heap this page has run the peak lands between about two thirds of the heap and a fifth above it. Every engine on a table gets the same memory envelope; how much of it a JVM takes is a property of the runtime, so read these cells against each other rather than against an engine that manages its own memory.

Each repetition runs every read against a fresh set of start persons (SF1 (10k people, 181k friendships): 500, SF10 (66k people, 1.9M friendships): 200) and 1,000 each of the insert, update, and delete; the p50 and p99 are over those.

FalkorDB at SF1 (10k people, 181k friendships) and SF10 (66k people, 1.9M friendships): its disk cells are 0.0 because the server container did not grow over its empty footprint during the run: at the relaxed setting FalkorDB persists only by timed snapshots, with no append-only file, and none had been taken when disk was measured, so the graph was held in memory only; read them as a floor under 0.01 GiB, not as a size.

Ingest paths: ArcadeDB embedded loads through the Java API (newVertex, newEdge) in 5,000-record transactions; served sends CREATE VERTEX and CREATE EDGE statements as sqlscript batches over HTTP; Neo4j and Memgraph UNWIND batches over bolt; FalkorDB the same UNWIND batches over the Redis protocol; LadybugDB COPY from CSV, its native bulk path; DuckPGQ registers each batch as an Arrow table and INSERT ... SELECTs from it into the Person and knows tables, then defines the property graph over them; ArangoDB import_bulk; MongoDB insert_many; SurrealDB inserts the persons through its Python SDK and the KNOWS edges as bulk relation inserts.

tables.title: Cross-model transaction: what survives a crash
tables.dataset: The same vector-graph-document operation, killed mid-way, then inspected
conditions: A trial writes the three products, kills the process between them, reopens, and checks whether every product is present or none. Torn means some but not all: the counts the page's E2 prose quotes are these.

SurrealDB (embedded) at 500k products: the atomicity cell exceeded its 2 hour budget, the same budget every engine on this table had, on its first attempt and was not retried; there is no row. It was still in the index build when the budget ran out.
In the cells: `>2h` means the cell ran past its tier's cap and was not retried. A dash is an operation the engine cannot express, never a slow one.

tables.title: Cross-model transaction
tables.dataset: Vector hit to graph traversal to document update, in one transaction
conditions: The engines do not all run the same SHAPE of filtered search, and it shows in the recall column as much as the time one. ArangoDB, MongoDB, Neo4j (vector index), PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE, Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction), SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) restrict the candidate set first and rank what is left by distance, so they return that set's true nearest matches. ArcadeDB (one transaction) and ArcadeDB (server, one transaction) instead take an over-large global top-k and keep whichever candidates happen to fall inside it: more work, and a partial answer, because a global list of that size usually does not contain enough of the candidates. Read both columns for those arms as what this query shape costs rather than as what the engine can do.

The transaction is the update, and every engine here commits it all or nothing. ArcadeDB (one transaction), ArcadeDB (server, one transaction), Neo4j (vector index), and PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE also run the vector search and the hop inside it; ArangoDB, MongoDB, SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) run those two reads first and wrap only the update (MongoDB cannot do otherwise: it refuses a vector search inside a multi-document transaction, and its rows record the refusal). One client runs at a time, so the answers are the same either way. Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction) has no transaction spanning its two systems, which is what that row exists to show.
Disk is what the workload left on disk, in GiB: the engine's writable layer plus its volumes after the cell, minus the same engine's empty footprint.

SurrealDB's graph-filtered search is marked `re-run`: our query scanned every product instead of reading the candidates by record id, the access path every other engine on this table was given. It is being re-measured with the fix.

SurrealDB (server) retrieval at the 500k tier is marked `re-run`: the server was still building its vector index in the background when these queries ran. It is being re-measured with the build waiting for the index to catch up.

Qdrant + Neo4j's row is marked `re-run`. Its vector half ran in the Qdrant client's in-memory local mode, a pure-Python reimplementation rather than the Qdrant server, so every time, recall, and disk value it produced described that reimplementation. It is being re-run against the Qdrant server the vector table uses. Its all-or-nothing result on the table above does not depend on this.
There is no cold column on this table, and the reason is recorded on the rows themselves: no cold/warm split: each operation runs against an already-built, already-warm database by construction

Durability is matched at the relaxed end: on every engine that has the setting, a commit returns without waiting for the disk and the log is flushed by the engine's own background policy, which is ArcadeDB's engine default and a documented production mode for each of the others. Every engine's setting was read out of the engine rather than assumed, and each row records what it ran as `durability`. The exception on this table is Neo4j, Neo4j (vector index), and Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction), which have no setting to relax and wait for the disk at every commit; their write and transaction cells are paying for that. SurrealDB (server) exposes no durability setting at all and what it does at commit could not be established, so it is in neither class and its row says so rather than claiming one.

Atomic means all or nothing: the whole update happens, or none of it does, with no state in between that anyone can observe. One engine can promise that across a vector, a graph edge, and a document because they share a transaction. Qdrant and Neo4j cannot promise it to each other, because nothing spans the two.

So the interesting result here is not the speed. It is what a crash halfway through leaves behind. The raw data records, for each run, whether an interrupted write left the two stores disagreeing, and whether they still disagreed after restarting. That is what this comparison exists to show.
SurrealDB embedded runs on the SDK's SurrealKV store on disk and SurrealDB server on RocksDB, and each has its own disk reading.

ArcadeDB (one transaction), ArcadeDB (server, one transaction), and Neo4j (vector index) run on a JVM, and for them this column is close to the heap they were given rather than the memory the work needed: Neo4j (vector index)'s 6.83 GiB here is about 114 per cent of its 6g heap, and across every heap this page has run the peak lands between about two thirds of the heap and a fifth above it. Every engine on a table gets the same memory envelope; how much of it a JVM takes is a property of the runtime, so read these cells against each other rather than against an engine that manages its own memory.
Each repetition runs the transaction 300 times; the p50 and p99 are over those.

Indexes on this table are matched by effect rather than by rule: ArangoDB, ArcadeDB (one transaction), ArcadeDB (server, one transaction), MongoDB, Neo4j (vector index), PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE, SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) build one. Where building one was a choice, the engine was timed with it and without it and the faster configuration kept; where an engine reaches these queries through its own primary key or record id, that is its equivalent. The time an index took to build is the index column.

SurrealDB (embedded) at 500k products: the transaction cell exceeded its 2 hour budget, the same budget every engine on this table had, on its first attempt and was not retried; there is no row. It was still in the index build when the budget ran out.

In the cells: `>2h` means the cell ran past its tier's cap and was not retried. `re-run` means the cell was measured before a fix to our harness and is being measured again; the note says what was wrong. A dash is an operation the engine cannot express, never a slow one.

ingest+index total s is one timer around loading the vertices and edges and creating the vector index. tables.title: What waiting for the disk costs
tables.dataset: Every timed write, run twice, once at each durability setting
conditions: Each row is one engine running ONE operation twice: once where a commit returns without waiting for the disk, which is the setting every other table on this page reports, and once where the commit waits for the log to be flushed and synced. Nothing else about the cell changes.

Every timed write on the page is here: the six document operations, the three graph writes, and the cross-model transaction. Read down the operations for one engine rather than across the engines for one operation, because what the setting costs is a property of the engine's commit and the rest of the page already compares the engines.
The read is the control, and it is the row that makes the rest readable: it runs in both cells like everything else and commits nothing, so it is what the writes are moving against.

The Size column names the operation rather than a corpus size: the three lanes that time a write do not write the same thing, so each engine is compared only against the engines running its own operation.
The setting is a property of the cell, not a second measurement inside one: it lives on the database or on the server for most of these engines, so each pair of numbers is two runs.

DuckDB, DuckPGQ, LadybugDB, Neo4j, Neo4j (vector index), and Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction) have no setting to relax, established by tracing the commits rather than assumed, so each prints one number, in the column for a commit that waits. Reading it against the other column would be reading a choice the engine does not offer.

SurrealDB (server) has no durability setting to read and what it does at commit could not be established from the engine, so the one number printed is in neither class. It is placed in the waiting column because that is the safer reading of an unknown, and this line is why it is there.

ArcadeDB (one transaction) shows almost no cost of waiting because of a defect in the engine build measured here, ArcadeDB issue #8129 (https://github.com/ArcadeData/arcadedb/issues/8129): after the vector index is built, later commits in the same session skip the write-ahead log, so there is nothing to wait for, and ArcadeDB 26.10.1 fixes it.

The ratio is what the strict setting costs on that engine, at this corpus size and this operation count. It is not a claim about any other write. A large ratio is not a slow engine: it is an engine whose relaxed path was fast, measured against a flush that costs what a flush costs.

tables.title: What the client/server split costs
conditions: Measured at ArcadeDB 26.10.1.dev0 on 2026-09-21. This table has not yet been re-run at the engine commit the rest of the page reports; the re-run is queued and this line goes away with it.
Every number is milliseconds. One engine build (arcadedb 26.10.1-dev · 417314c18) in all three deployments, 15 repetitions after 3 warmup, identical cpuset 0-11, memory cap 8g and heap 6g.
All three deployments turn the answer into Python objects the same way, so the difference is how the database was deployed and not how we read the result.

The separate container runs on the same machine, talking over the local network interface. It says what running the database beside your program costs, and says nothing about a database on another machine across a real network.

The separate-process column goes slightly negative at the smaller result sizes. That is not a container being faster than an in-process server; it is the boundary term sitting below what this design can resolve, so run-to-run noise swamps it and the sign flips. Reported rather than clamped to zero, because the negative values are the evidence for the claim: at these sizes co-locating costs nothing measurable. The packing cost, in the column beside it, stays firmly positive at every size.

tables.title: Document OLTP
tables.dataset: TPC-C new-order on the TPC-H tables (SF1, SF10)
conditions: Six transactional operations. New-order: TPC-C's checkout transaction: it reads a customer and a warehouse, inserts an order with its line items, and updates stock, all in one transaction. Payment: TPC-C's payment against one of the orders new-order just placed, chosen at random: the order is read, marked paid, and the payment inserted, in one transaction. Insert: one record inserted by key. Read: one record read back by key. Update: one record's quantity updated by key. Delete: one record deleted by key. OLTP ops/s is the rate of the two TPC-C transactions together; the four single-record operations are timed one at a time.
Disk is what the workload left on disk, in GiB: the engine's writable layer plus its volumes after the cell, minus the same engine's empty footprint.
There is no cold column on this table, and the reason is recorded on the rows themselves: no cold/warm split: each operation runs against an already-built, already-warm database by construction

Durability is matched at the relaxed end: on every engine that has the setting, a commit returns without waiting for the disk and the log is flushed by the engine's own background policy, which is ArcadeDB's engine default and a documented production mode for each of the others. Every engine's setting was read out of the engine rather than assumed, and each row records what it ran as `durability`. The exception on this table is DuckDB, which has no setting to relax and waits for the disk at every commit; its write and transaction cells are paying for that. SurrealDB (server) exposes no durability setting at all and what it does at commit could not be established, so it is in neither class and its row says so rather than claiming one.

PostgreSQL's memory cell is not comparable to the others: this column counts memory an engine holds in its own address space, and PostgreSQL holds its data in shared memory and the kernel's file cache instead. At TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items), of the 1.54 GiB shown, 1.464 GiB is our Python client and 0.070 GiB is the database.

ArcadeDB (embedded) and ArcadeDB (server) run on a JVM, and for them this column is close to the heap they were given rather than the memory the work needed: ArcadeDB (server)'s 6.42 GiB here is about 80 per cent of its 8g heap, and across every heap this page has run the peak lands between about two thirds of the heap and a fifth above it. Every engine on a table gets the same memory envelope; how much of it a JVM takes is a property of the runtime, so read these cells against each other rather than against an engine that manages its own memory.

Each repetition runs 1,000 new-order transactions and 1,000 payments, then 1,000 each of the single-record insert, read, update, and delete; the p50 and p99 are over those, and OLTP ops/s is the rate of the two transactions together.

SurrealDB (embedded) at TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items): the transaction cell reached the 32g memory envelope (peak 32,768 MiB) and was killed by the kernel, the same envelope every engine on this table had; it did not run out of time, and there is no row.
In the cells: `OOM` means killed at the cell's memory envelope rather than running out of time. A dash is an operation the engine cannot express, never a slow one.

Ingest paths: ArcadeDB embedded loads through the Python package's insert_many in 10,000-row batches, one JSON payload per batch; served sends INSERT statements as sqlscript batches over HTTP; PostgreSQL COPY FROM STDIN; DuckDB CREATE TABLE AS SELECT from in-memory frames; SQLite executemany; MongoDB insert_many; ArangoDB import_bulk; SurrealDB inserts through its Python SDK.

tables.title: Document OLAP
tables.dataset: TPC-H Q1, Q6, top parts, ship mode, and by month (SF1, SF10)
conditions: Five analytical queries, each over the whole line-item table. Q1: TPC-H's own Q1, the pricing summary: it groups and aggregates every line item, so it measures a full scan. Q6: TPC-H's own Q6, the forecasting revenue change: it sums one column under a narrow filter, so it measures how well an engine skips what it does not need. Top parts: the ten parts with the highest revenue, a group-by over every line item with a sort and a limit. Ship mode: how many line items went by each ship mode, a group-by over the whole table. By month: revenue by month of shipment, a group-by on a date expression. All times are milliseconds.
Disk is what the workload left on disk, in GiB: the engine's writable layer plus its volumes after the cell, minus the same engine's empty footprint.

The cold column is the very first query of a session, TPC-H Q1, timed once on a database that has just been opened; every other latency column is the warm median of the iterations that follow it. It answers what the first query of a session costs against the hundredth, which is a different question from the steady-state one and is the one an application that opens a database per request actually asks.

Durability is matched at the relaxed end: on every engine that has the setting, a commit returns without waiting for the disk and the log is flushed by the engine's own background policy, which is ArcadeDB's engine default and a documented production mode for each of the others. Every engine's setting was read out of the engine rather than assumed, and each row records what it ran as `durability`. The exception on this table is DuckDB, which has no setting to relax and waits for the disk at every commit; its write and transaction cells are paying for that. SurrealDB (server) exposes no durability setting at all and what it does at commit could not be established, so it is in neither class and its row says so rather than claiming one.

PostgreSQL's memory cell is not comparable to the others: this column counts memory an engine holds in its own address space, and PostgreSQL holds its data in shared memory and the kernel's file cache instead. At TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items), of the 1.54 GiB shown, 1.464 GiB is our Python client and 0.070 GiB is the database.

ArcadeDB (embedded) and ArcadeDB (server) run on a JVM, and for them this column is close to the heap they were given rather than the memory the work needed: ArcadeDB (server)'s 6.42 GiB here is about 80 per cent of its 8g heap, and across every heap this page has run the peak lands between about two thirds of the heap and a fifth above it. Every engine on a table gets the same memory envelope; how much of it a JVM takes is a property of the runtime, so read these cells against each other rather than against an engine that manages its own memory.
Each repetition runs every query 100 times; the p50 and p99 are over those runs.

Indexes on this table are matched by effect rather than by rule: ArcadeDB (embedded), ArcadeDB (server), MongoDB, PostgreSQL, SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) build one; ArangoDB, DuckDB, and SQLite build none, because measuring it showed the index costs them or changes nothing. Where building one was a choice, the engine was timed with it and without it and the faster configuration kept; where an engine reaches these queries through its own primary key or record id, that is its equivalent. The time an index took to build is the index column.

SurrealDB (embedded) and SurrealDB (server) at TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items): the analytics cell reached the 32g memory envelope (peak 32,768 MiB) and was killed by the kernel, the same envelope every engine on this table had; it did not run out of time, and there is no row.

30 query cells on this table stopped at their per-query budget, the same for every engine here; each one's p50 and p99 are over those iterations, the first of which is the cold pass, and every other query in those cells keeps its numbers.

ArangoDB at TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items): Q1 (49 of 100 iterations, reaching 867 to 871 s), Q6 (66 to 67, reaching 866 to 875 s), by month (76 to 78, reaching 864 to 874 s), and top parts (35 to 36, reaching 864 to 888 s).

ArcadeDB (embedded) at TPC-H SF10 (60.0M line items): Q1 (1 of 100 iterations, reaching 562 to 569 s), Q6 (12, reaching 888 to 899 s), by month (13 to 14, reaching 866 to 924 s), ship mode (21, reaching 869 to 887 s), and top parts (9, reaching 868 to 890 s).

The engines do not all run the same SHAPE of filtered search, and it shows in the recall column as much as the time one. ArangoDB, MongoDB, Neo4j (vector index), PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE, Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction), SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) restrict the candidate set first and rank what is left by distance, so they return that set's true nearest matches. ArcadeDB (one transaction) and ArcadeDB (server, one transaction) instead take an over-large global top-k and keep whichever candidates happen to fall inside it: more work, and a partial answer, because a global list of that size usually does not contain enough of the candidates. Read both columns for those arms as what this query shape costs rather than as what the engine can do.

The transaction is the update, and every engine here commits it all or nothing. ArcadeDB (one transaction), ArcadeDB (server, one transaction), Neo4j (vector index), and PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE also run the vector search and the hop inside it; ArangoDB, MongoDB, SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) run those two reads first and wrap only the update (MongoDB cannot do otherwise: it refuses a vector search inside a multi-document transaction, and its rows record the refusal). One client runs at a time, so the answers are the same either way. Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction) has no transaction spanning its two systems, which is what that row exists to show.

Six transactional operations. New-order: TPC-C's checkout transaction: it reads a customer and a warehouse, inserts an order with its line items, and updates stock, all in one transaction. Payment: TPC-C's payment against one of the orders new-order just placed, chosen at random: the order is read, marked paid, and the payment inserted, in one transaction. Insert: one record inserted by key. Read: one record read back by key. Update: one record's quantity updated by key. Delete: one record deleted by key. OLTP ops/s is the rate of the two TPC-C transactions together; the four single-record operations are timed one at a time.

PostgreSQL's memory cell is not comparable to the others: this column counts memory an engine holds in its own address space, and PostgreSQL holds its data in shared memory and the kernel's file cache instead. Five analytical queries, each over the whole line-item table. Q1: TPC-H's own Q1, the pricing summary: it groups and aggregates every line item, so it measures a full scan. Q6: TPC-H's own Q6, the forecasting revenue change: it sums one column under a narrow filter, so it measures how well an engine skips what it does not need. Top parts: the ten parts with the highest revenue, a group-by over every line item with a sort and a limit. Ship mode: how many line items went by each ship mode, a group-by over the whole table. By month: revenue by month of shipment, a group-by on a date expression. All times are milliseconds.
Each repetition runs every query 100 times; the p50 and p99 are over those runs.
